Article Title: 'All out of control': Spain invokes first wildfire emergency as fires rage across Europe; over 10,000 evacuated
Article Text:
A wall of flames advances as a wildfire burns near Burgohondo, in Ávila province, Spain (Picture credit: AP)

First wildfire emergency in Spain

France asks EU for firefighting aircraft

Poll Vote & Share your view How concerned are you about the increasing intensity of wildfires in southern Europe? Very concerned Not concerned at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Heatwave and climate concerns

Spain declared a national emergency over wildfires for the first time on Friday, while France requested European Union assistance to battle a major blaze on its Atlantic coast, as an intense heatwave drove destructive fires across southern Europe and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people.The emergency declaration in Spain followed multiple uncontrolled fires around Madrid and in neighbouring Ávila province, prompting authorities to evacuate more than 10,000 residents from towns in the mountains west of the capital.The measure allows Spain's interior ministry to take charge of coordinating firefighting operations nationwide.French authorities ordered the full evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula, a popular tourist destination near Bordeaux, where around 40,000 people were forced to leave campsites, holiday homes and residential areas, with many evacuated by boat.Spanish officials said this was the first time the country had activated its highest level of emergency specifically for a wildfire. The same level had previously been used during a nationwide power blackout last year.More than 270 emergency personnel, 40 ground units and several contingents from Spain's Military Emergency Unit have been deployed to the affected areas.In Navaluenga, one of the worst-hit towns in Ávila province, residents watched helicopters scoop water from the local river as smoke filled the air."I've lived here for 36 years and I've never seen anything like it. Nor did I expect it. I thought they were going to get it under control last night, but it was already late, and it was all out of control," resident Javier Martin told Reuters.According to the EU's European Forest Fire Information Service (EFFIS), more than 350 fires have burned in Spain so far this year. About 1,300 square kilometres have already been destroyed, more than four times the area burned during the same period last year.Spain has also suffered its second-largest wildfire on record this year, which burned roughly 320 square kilometres in Guadalajara province north of Madrid.Earlier this month, 13 people were killed in a fire in southern Spain, the country's deadliest wildfire in recent memory.The Cap Ferret fire has already burned about 8,700 hectares, or 87 square kilometres, making it one of France's most serious blazes in recent years.President Emmanuel Macron announced that France had activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism and requested additional firefighting resources from European partners."France has requested the activation of the European Union's civil protection mechanism," Macron wrote on X, adding that specialist aircraft from several European countries were expected to arrive soon.The EU is sending two Croatian Canadair firefighting planes, two Portuguese Air Tractor aircraft and heavy-lift Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia.The blaze has spread through pine forests near Bordeaux's wine-growing region, turning the sky orange and filling nearby areas with smoke.Residents described hurried evacuations as flames approached homes."The gendarmes came and knocked on every door, the fire was about 500 metres away -- we grabbed some things and left," Patrick Martineau, a resident of Le Porge, told news agency AFP.Temperatures are expected to exceed 39°C in parts of southeastern Spain, with some areas forecast to reach 44°C.Smoke from the fires was reportedly noticeable in parts of Madrid on Friday morning.The crisis is part of a broader pattern of increasingly severe wildfires across southern Europe. EFFIS satellite data show that the total area burned across EU countries this year is already the second-largest on record.Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. Scientists say human-caused climate change is intensifying heatwaves and drought conditions, making the region more vulnerable to large, fast-moving fires.Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the situation "dramatic" and renewed his appeal for a political pact to tackle climate change, saying the country must adapt to a future of more frequent and intense wildfires.The fires have also taken a heavy toll on emergency responders.Three firefighters have died during wildfire operations in southern Europe in recent days, including two who were killed while battling a blaze near Bordeaux airport earlier this week.
Article Summary: Spain declares national emergency over wildfires for the first time. France requests EU assistance to battle a major blaze on its Atlantic coast. More than 350 fires have burned in Spain so far this year, more than four times the area burned in the same period last year.

Article Title: US man gets two life terms for killing ex-Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman, husband
Article Text:
Pictures of Mark and Melissa Hortman inside the sanctuary at the Basilica of St. Mary's during their funeral (Photo: AP).

A US District Court on Thursday sentenced Vance Boelter to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years in prison for the fatal shooting of former Minnesota Democratic lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark Hortman, in a politically motivated attack.Boelter was also convicted of critically injuring state senator John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, along with two counts of attempted murder, impersonating a police officer and animal cruelty.Nearly a year after the Minneapolis-area attacks, Boelter agreed to plead guilty in June for fear of federal prosecutors seeking the death penalty.On June 14, 2025, Vance Boelter reportedly rang the doorbell to Hortman’s home at around 3:30 am, disguised as a police officer on a welfare check, wearing a uniform and a mask.Once Mark Hortman answered the door, Boelter gave him a fake name and badge number before requesting him to summon Melissa Hortman, following which he killed both of them, shooting multiple times.According to police, Boelter had already visited the Hoffmans’, shooting and critically injuring the senator and his wife. In failed attempts, he reportedly also went to two other lawmakers’ houses that night.“My days are filled with grey, and the blood that was spilt is the last thing I see before I go to sleep and the first thing I see when I wake,” said Colin, son of the Hortmans, while speaking to CNN“There is no sentence that weighs 15 gunshots, a murdered dog and the rest of my life”, he added.Speaking to CNN, state senator John Hoffman shared what he experienced on the night of the incident.“The defendant looked me in the eyes and pulled the trigger. The defendant looked at my wife and chose to do the same,” Hoffman said, adding that he and his wife now live with the injuries, with their bodies remembering the gunfire.According to CNN, Boelter admitted to identifying and stalking his targets for months before carrying out the attacks.
Article Summary: Vance Boelter sentenced to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years in prison. Former Minnesota Democratic lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark Hortman, were killed in a politically motivated attack.Boelter also convicted of critically injuring state senator John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, along with two counts of attempted murder.

Article Title: US government's plans for $100,000 fee on new H-1B work visas rejected by court again; says: Government failed to show that ...
Article Text:
US appeals court keeps lower court ruling in place



US introduced $100K H-1B visa fees in 2025

A federal appeals court has rejected the US government's proposed fees of $100,000 on new H-1B work visas, saying the government failed to show that it was likely to succeed in proving that President Donald Trump had the authority to impose the charge. The ruling keeps in place a lower court's decision blocking the fee that was first introduced in 2025 as part of the Trump administration's broader immigration crackdown. The proposed fee would have sharply increased the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers, especially in the technology sector.As stated in a Business Insider report, the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston declined to pause a June ruling by US District Judge Leo Sorokin while the Trump administration appeals the case. The decision means the lower court ruling will remain in effect while the legal challenge continues.In his June decision, Judge Sorokin said the proposed fee was effectively a tax, and under the US Constitution, only Congress has the authority to impose taxes."Here, the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Sorokin then wrote.President Trump announced the fee in September 2025, saying the H-1B visa programme had been "deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, American workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labor."The H-1B programme allows US companies to hire highly skilled foreign professionals in specialised fields such as technology, engineering and healthcare. Each year, the programme issues 65,000 regular H-1B visas, along with 20,000 additional visas for applicants with advanced degrees from US universities.Before the proposed policy, employers typically paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in visa-related fees. According to court filings, demand for new H-1B visas dropped sharply after the administration announced the $100,000 fee. By mid-February, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services had received only a small number of payments under the new policy.
Article Summary: US appeals court keeps lower court ruling in place blocking $100K H-1B visa fees. The fee was first introduced in 2025 as part of the Trump administration's broader immigration crackdown. The proposed fee would have sharply increased the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers, especially in the technology sector.

Article Title: US government announces new global visa restriction policy; says: United States will go after those who ...
Article Text:
"The United States will go after those who prey on our citizens,”

“This policy targets individuals responsible for, or complicit in, cybercrime and cyber-enabled crime, such as those involved in cyberscams, and sextortion. Immediate family members of individuals engaged in such illicit activities may also be subjected to visa restrictions."

US has announced a new global visa restriction policy. The latest policy targets individuals involved in cybercrime and cyber-enabled offences. This includes applicants who will be found involved with online investment scams and sextortion. Announcing the measure, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the policy could also apply to immediate family members of those responsible for or complicit in such activities.he added.The new policy, introduced under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, is part of the Trump administration's broader efforts to combat international cybercrime networks. In a statement, Rubio said,The US State Department's new cybercrime visa policy expands its use of visa restrictions as a deterrent beyond immigration violations.Similar measures this year have targeted individuals accused of supporting political violence, aiding adversaries, cartel networks or undermining regional stability, with family members also facing restrictions.The US State Department's new cybercrime visa policy expands its use of visa restrictions as a deterrent beyond immigration violations. Similar measures this year have targeted individuals accused of supporting political violence, aiding adversaries, cartel networks or undermining regional stability, with family members also facing restrictions.The policy is part of broader efforts to tighten the visa system, both before and after applications are filed.The State Department has expanded online presence vetting for student and exchange visitor applicants, stating that visa adjudications are treated as national security decisions. It has also expanded visa bonds for some business and tourist applicants from countries associated with overstay risk.Public records show that cyber-enabled crime is frequently transnational and that foreign suspects are brought into U.S. courts, but they do not offer a clear public count of cybercriminals who obtained US visas.DOJ records include foreign nationals extradited in cyber-enabled fraud and extortion cases, as well as those arrested at US airports in cryptocurrency fraud prosecutions, but these records generally do not specify visa status. The State Department says thousands of people attempt to illegally obtain U.S. visas each year to commit crimes or evade prosecution, though it does not publish a cybercrime-specific breakdown.US officials have pointed to cyber campaigns called “Salt Typhoon” and “Volt Typhoon” CISA, FBI and NSA assessments have identified Chinese-linked actors associated with these campaigns who have sought to establish long-term access to telecommunications and other critical infrastructure networks to facilitate intelligence collection and possibly position themselves to disrupt systems during a future crisis. The agencies describe this as part of a broader strategy to embed within critical networks rather than conduct short-term intrusions.The FBI has previously said actors linked to "Salt Typhoon" compromised telecommunications providers as part of a cyberespionage operation affecting communications infrastructure. In a recent advisory, the bureau said Chinese-affiliated actors had targeted telecommunications networks globally and called on organisations to strengthen defences against long-term infiltration attempts.
Article Summary: US has announced a new global visa restriction policy. The latest policy targets individuals involved in cybercrime and cyber-enabled offences. This includes applicants who will be found involved with online investment scams and sextortion. The policy could also apply to immediate family members of those responsible for or complicit in such activities.
